lock.screen.name: Screen lock
lock.screen.titlePass: The screen locks when you are away
lock.screen.titleFail: The screen does not lock soon enough
lock.screen.why: An unlocked PC left alone gives anyone who walks by your files, mail and saved passwords.
fix: Open Settings > System > Power & battery and set the screen and sleep times to 15 minutes or less.
Open Settings > Accounts > Sign-in options and have Windows ask you to sign in again every time you were away.
Lock by hand with Windows+L whenever you leave your desk.

logon.automatic.name: Automatic sign-in
logon.automatic.titlePass: Windows asks who you are at start-up
logon.automatic.titleFail: Windows signs in automatically at start-up
logon.automatic.why: With automatic sign-in, anyone who turns the PC on is signed in as you. The password is also kept on the PC in readable form.
fix: Press Windows+R, type netplwiz and press Enter.
Tick "Users must enter a user name and password to use this computer" and select OK.
Change your password, since the old one was stored on the PC.

accounts.builtin.name: Built-in accounts
accounts.builtin.titlePass: The built-in Administrator and Guest accounts are off
accounts.builtin.why: Every Windows PC has these two accounts, so attackers try them first. Guest needs no password at all.
fix: Press Windows+R, type lusrmgr.msc and press Enter, then open Users.
Open the account shown as enabled, tick "Account is disabled" and select OK.
On Windows Home, which has no such tool, ask IT to disable the account.

password.manager.name: Password manager
password.manager.why: A password manager makes a long, different password for every site practical. Reused passwords are how one leak becomes many break-ins.
fix: Install the password manager your organisation provides, or ask IT which one to use.
Add its browser extension and move your saved passwords into it.

ssh.keys.passphrase.name: SSH key passphrases
ssh.keys.passphrase.titleFail: An SSH key has no passphrase
ssh.keys.passphrase.why: An SSH key without a passphrase works for anyone who copies the file. Malware looks for these files first.
fix: Open a terminal.
Run ssh-keygen -p -f followed by the path of the key file, and enter a new passphrase.
Or move the key into a password manager or SSH agent and delete the file.

ssh.keys.strength.name: SSH key strength
ssh.keys.strength.why: Short RSA keys and DSA keys can be broken with enough computing power, and current servers refuse some of them.
fix: Open a terminal and run ssh-keygen -t ed25519 to create a new key.
Add the new public key wherever the old one was used.
Remove the old key from those places, then delete its files.

ssh.config.name: SSH client settings
ssh.config.why: Forwarding your agent lets every server you connect to use your keys. Without host key checking, an impostor server goes unnoticed.
fix: Open the settings file named in the details in a text editor.
Remove ForwardAgent from settings that apply to every host; use ProxyJump or set it for one host.
Remove "StrictHostKeyChecking no" and "UserKnownHostsFile /dev/null" from settings that apply to every host.

updates.automatic.name: Automatic updates
updates.automatic.titleFail: Windows updates are off or paused
updates.automatic.why: Most attacks use flaws that an update has already fixed. Updates that wait for you to remember them arrive too late.
fix: Open Settings > Windows Update.
Select Resume updates if updates are paused.
If the page says your organisation manages updates and they stay off, contact IT.

updates.recent.name: Recent updates
updates.recent.titleFail: Windows has not been updated recently
updates.recent.why: Microsoft releases security fixes every month. A PC that has installed nothing for longer is missing them.
fix: Open Settings > Windows Update and select Check for updates.
Install what is offered and restart when asked.
If updates fail to install, note the error shown and contact IT.

updates.restart.name: Restart
updates.restart.why: Many updates only take effect after a restart. Until then the PC keeps running the old, flawed code.
fix: Save your work.
Open Start, select the power button and choose Update and restart, or Restart.

updates.supported.name: Windows version
updates.supported.titlePass: This Windows version still gets security updates
updates.supported.titleFail: This Windows version no longer gets security updates
updates.supported.why: Once a Windows version reaches its end date, newly found flaws stay open for good.
fix: Open Settings > Windows Update and install the newer Windows version offered there.
If none is offered, the PC may not meet its requirements: contact IT.

updates.secreview.name: SecReview up to date
updates.secreview.titleFail: A newer version of SecReview is available
updates.secreview.why: New versions add checks and fix mistakes in old ones. An old SecReview can call a PC safe that is not.
fix: Open SecReview and choose Update now on the notice at the top.
If there is no such button, your organisation installs updates: tell IT.

firewall.enabled.name: Firewall
firewall.enabled.why: A firewall stops other devices on the same network from reaching your PC. It matters most on public Wi-Fi.
fix: Open Windows Security and select Firewall & network protection.
Select each network shown as off and turn Microsoft Defender Firewall on.

remote.desktop.name: Remote Desktop
remote.desktop.titlePass: Remote Desktop is off or asks for sign-in first
remote.desktop.titleFail: Remote Desktop accepts connections without sign-in first
remote.desktop.why: Remote Desktop lets other computers control this PC. Without Network Level Authentication, anyone on the network reaches the sign-in screen and its flaws.
fix: Open Settings > System > Remote Desktop.
Turn Remote Desktop off if you do not use it.
Otherwise open its options and require Network Level Authentication.

remote.services.name: Remote management services
remote.services.titlePass: No remote management service is running
remote.services.titleFail: A remote management service is running
remote.services.why: These services let other computers run commands on this PC. A staff PC rarely needs them, and each one is another door to guard.
fix: Press Windows+R, type services.msc and press Enter.
Open the service shown as running, select Stop and set Startup type to Disabled.
If you need the service for your work, tell IT instead.

sharing.folders.name: Shared folders
sharing.folders.titlePass: No folders are shared on the network
sharing.folders.titleFail: Folders are shared on the network
sharing.folders.why: A shared folder is reachable from every network the PC joins, including public Wi-Fi if the firewall allows it.
fix: Press Windows+R, type fsmgmt.msc and press Enter, then open Shares.
Right-click each share you no longer need and select Stop Sharing.
Leave the shares whose names end in $: Windows uses them itself.

disk.encryption.name: Disk encryption
disk.encryption.why: Without encryption, anyone who takes the PC or its drive can read every file on it.
fix: Open Settings > Privacy & security > Device encryption and turn it on.
If that page is missing, search for Manage BitLocker and turn BitLocker on for each drive.
Store the recovery key where your organisation asks you to.
disk.encryption.timeToFix: 10 min, then encrypts in the background

antivirus.active.name: Antivirus
antivirus.active.titleFail: Antivirus is off or out of date
antivirus.active.why: Antivirus blocks known malware before it runs. Out-of-date definitions miss recent threats.
fix: Open Windows Security and select Virus & threat protection.
Turn real-time protection on, or follow the action shown for your antivirus.
Select Protection updates and check for updates.

defender.protection.name: Microsoft Defender protection
defender.protection.titleFail: A Microsoft Defender protection is off
defender.protection.why: Real-time and cloud protection catch malware as it arrives. Tamper protection stops malware from switching them off.
fix: Open Windows Security and select Virus & threat protection.
Under Virus & threat protection settings, select Manage settings.
Turn on Real-time protection, Cloud-delivered protection and Tamper Protection.

system.uac.name: User Account Control
system.uac.titlePass: Windows asks before programs get administrator rights
system.uac.titleFail: Programs get administrator rights without asking
system.uac.why: With User Account Control off, every program you start can change Windows itself without you noticing.
fix: Open Start, type UAC and open Change User Account Control settings.
Move the slider to the second position from the top, or to the top, and select OK.
Restart the PC.

system.secureboot.name: Secure Boot
system.secureboot.why: Secure Boot lets only trusted software start the PC. Without it, malware can load before Windows and hide from it.
fix: Open Settings > System > Recovery and select Restart now next to Advanced startup.
Choose Troubleshoot > Advanced options > UEFI Firmware Settings and restart.
Turn Secure Boot on, save and exit. If the PC then fails to start, turn it off again and ask IT.

system.tpm.name: Security chip (TPM)
system.tpm.titlePass: The PC has a TPM 2.0 security chip
system.tpm.titleFail: The PC has no usable TPM 2.0 security chip
system.tpm.why: The TPM keeps disk encryption keys and sign-in secrets out of reach of software. Without it they are easier to steal.
fix: Open Settings > System > Recovery and select Restart now next to Advanced startup.
Choose Troubleshoot > Advanced options > UEFI Firmware Settings and restart.
Turn the TPM on; it may be called PTT or fTPM. If there is no such setting, tell IT.

system.memoryintegrity.name: Memory integrity
system.memoryintegrity.why: Memory integrity stops malicious or flawed drivers from changing Windows' own code while it runs.
fix: Open Windows Security and select Device security > Core isolation details.
Turn Memory integrity on and restart.
If Windows lists incompatible drivers, update or remove them first.

system.bootoptions.name: Start-up protections
system.bootoptions.titlePass: Windows starts with its normal protections
system.bootoptions.titleFail: Windows starts in a developer mode
system.bootoptions.why: Test signing lets unsigned drivers load, and kernel debugging gives full control over Windows. Both are for driver developers only.
fix: Open a terminal as administrator.
Run bcdedit /set testsigning off, then bcdedit /debug off.
Restart the PC.

sc.uv.cooldown.name: uv release cooldown
sc.uv.cooldown.titlePass: uv waits before installing new releases
sc.uv.cooldown.titleFail: uv installs releases that are too new
sc.uv.cooldown.why: Most malicious package versions are found and removed within days. A week's wait keeps them off this PC.
fix: Open %APPDATA%\uv\uv.toml in a text editor; create the file if it is missing.
Add a line with exclude-newer = "7 days" and save.
Update uv if it is older than 0.9.17, with uv self update or the way you installed it.

sc.uv.sources.name: uv package sources
sc.uv.sources.titlePass: uv gets packages only from verified sources
sc.uv.sources.titleFail: uv is set to trust unsafe package sources
sc.uv.sources.why: These settings decide which servers uv believes. One weak setting lets an attacker's package stand in for the real one.
fix: Open the file, or the environment variable, named in the details.
Remove the setting shown there, so uv's own default applies again.
For a private index, give it a name and mark it explicit rather than changing the index strategy.

sc.uv.credentials.name: uv stored sign-ins
sc.uv.credentials.titlePass: uv keeps no sign-in secrets as plain text
sc.uv.credentials.titleFail: uv keeps sign-in secrets as plain text
sc.uv.credentials.why: A token in a plain file or a permanent variable can be read by every program you run, a malicious package's install step included.
fix: For a sign-in in uv's credentials file, run uv auth logout with the service named in the details.
For a variable, press Start, open Edit environment variables for your account and delete it.
Replace the token at the service, since it was stored in the open, and keep the new one in your password manager.

sc.pnpm.cooldown.name: pnpm release cooldown
sc.pnpm.cooldown.titlePass: pnpm waits before installing new releases
sc.pnpm.cooldown.titleFail: pnpm installs releases that are too new
sc.pnpm.cooldown.why: Most malicious package versions are found and removed within days. A week's wait keeps them off this PC.
fix: Open a terminal and run pnpm config set --global minimumReleaseAge 10080, which is 7 days in minutes.
Update pnpm if it is older than 10.16.

sc.pnpm.settings.name: pnpm protections
sc.pnpm.settings.titleFail: A pnpm protection is switched off
sc.pnpm.settings.why: These settings stop packages from running install scripts unasked and from arriving tampered with. Each one switched off is a way in.
fix: Open the file named in the details in a text editor.
Remove the setting shown there, so pnpm's own default applies again.
To allow one package to run its build script, list it under allowBuilds instead of allowing all.

sc.pnpm.credentials.name: pnpm stored tokens
sc.pnpm.credentials.titlePass: pnpm keeps no registry tokens as plain text
sc.pnpm.credentials.titleFail: pnpm keeps registry tokens as plain text
sc.pnpm.credentials.why: A registry token in a plain file or a permanent variable can be read by every program you run. With it, an attacker publishes packages in your name.
fix: Run pnpm logout for the registry named in the details, or delete the line shown there.
Revoke the token at the registry, since it was stored in the open.
For publishing, use a short-lived token or sign in again when needed.

sc.scoop.buckets.name: Scoop buckets
sc.scoop.buckets.titlePass: Scoop's buckets come from Scoop's own sources
sc.scoop.buckets.titleFail: A Scoop bucket comes from another source
sc.scoop.buckets.why: Scoop installs whatever a bucket's manifest names, and runs its install scripts. Whoever controls a bucket controls what lands on this PC.
fix: Decide whether you still need the bucket named in the details and trust who runs it.
If not, remove it with scoop bucket rm followed by its name.
If you keep it, tell IT, so the choice is a known one.

sc.scoop.apps.name: Scoop app downloads
sc.scoop.apps.titlePass: Scoop apps were verified when installed
sc.scoop.apps.titleFail: A Scoop app was not verified when installed
sc.scoop.apps.why: Without a hash, Scoop cannot tell a tampered download from the real one. An app with no bucket has no source to check it against later.
fix: Reinstall the app named in the details from one of Scoop's buckets: scoop uninstall, then scoop install.
If only a nightly or unverified build exists, weigh whether you need the app.

sc.scoop.updates.name: Scoop app updates
sc.scoop.updates.titlePass: Scoop apps are up to date
sc.scoop.updates.why: Scoop never updates by itself. An app stays at the version you installed, with its known flaws, until you update it.
fix: Open a terminal and run scoop update to refresh the buckets.
Run scoop update * to update every app, or scoop update followed by one app's name.

sc.scoop.credentials.name: Scoop stored tokens
sc.scoop.credentials.titlePass: Scoop keeps no tokens as plain text
sc.scoop.credentials.titleFail: Scoop keeps tokens as plain text
sc.scoop.credentials.why: Scoop's settings file is plain text that every program you run can read. A GitHub token in it gives them your GitHub access.
fix: Remove the setting named in the details with scoop config rm followed by its name.
Revoke the token where it was issued, since it was stored in the open.
If Scoop hits GitHub's rate limit without a token, create one with no permissions at all.

sc.npm.cooldown.name: npm release cooldown
sc.npm.cooldown.titlePass: npm waits before installing new releases
sc.npm.cooldown.titleFail: npm installs releases that are too new
sc.npm.cooldown.why: Most malicious package versions are found and removed within days. A week's wait keeps them off this PC.
fix: Open a terminal and run npm config set min-release-age 7, which is 7 days.
Update npm if it is older than 11.10, with npm install -g npm.

sc.yarn.cooldown.name: Yarn release cooldown
sc.yarn.cooldown.titlePass: Yarn waits before installing new releases
sc.yarn.cooldown.titleFail: Yarn installs releases that are too new
sc.yarn.cooldown.why: Most malicious package versions are found and removed within days. A week's wait keeps them off this PC.
fix: Open .yarnrc.yml in your user folder in a text editor; create the file if it is missing.
Add a line with npmMinimalAgeGate: "7d" and save.
Run yarn set version stable in each project whose Yarn is older than 4.10.

sc.bun.cooldown.name: Bun release cooldown
sc.bun.cooldown.titlePass: Bun waits before installing new releases
sc.bun.cooldown.titleFail: Bun installs releases that are too new
sc.bun.cooldown.why: Most malicious package versions are found and removed within days. A week's wait keeps them off this PC.
fix: Open .bunfig.toml in your user folder in a text editor; create the file if it is missing.
Under an [install] line, add minimumReleaseAge = 604800, which is 7 days in seconds, and save.
Run bun upgrade if your Bun is older than 1.3.

sc.pip.cooldown.name: pip release cooldown
sc.pip.cooldown.titlePass: pip waits before installing new releases
sc.pip.cooldown.titleFail: pip installs releases that are too new
sc.pip.cooldown.why: Most malicious package versions are found and removed within days. A week's wait keeps them off this PC.
fix: Open a terminal and run pip config set global.uploaded-prior-to P7D, which is 7 days.
Update pip to 26.1 or later in each Python, with python -m pip install --upgrade pip.

sc.poetry.cooldown.name: Poetry release cooldown
sc.poetry.cooldown.titlePass: Poetry waits before installing new releases
sc.poetry.cooldown.titleFail: Poetry installs releases that are too new
sc.poetry.cooldown.why: Most malicious package versions are found and removed within days. A week's wait keeps them off this PC.
fix: Open a terminal and run poetry config solver.min-release-age 7, which is 7 days.
Run poetry self update if your Poetry is older than 2.4.

sc.pdm.cooldown.name: PDM release cooldown
sc.pdm.cooldown.titlePass: PDM waits before installing new releases
sc.pdm.cooldown.titleFail: PDM installs releases that are too new
sc.pdm.cooldown.why: Most malicious package versions are found and removed within days. A week's wait keeps them off this PC.
fix: Open a terminal and run pdm config strategy.exclude-newer 7d, which is 7 days.
Run pdm self update if your PDM is older than 2.27.

sc.npm.settings.name: npm protections
sc.npm.settings.titleFail: An npm protection is switched off
sc.npm.settings.why: TLS checks and HTTPS make sure a package comes from the registry it claims. Install scripts are how most malicious packages do their damage.
fix: Open the .npmrc file named in the details in a text editor.
Delete the line shown there, so npm's own default applies again.
To let one package run its install script, allow that package in the project, not all of them.

sc.npm.credentials.name: npm stored tokens
sc.npm.credentials.titlePass: No npm registry tokens are stored as plain text
sc.npm.credentials.titleFail: npm registry tokens are stored as plain text
sc.npm.credentials.why: A registry token in a plain file or a permanent variable can be read by every program you run. With it, an attacker publishes packages in your name.
fix: Run npm logout for the registry named in the details, or delete the line or variable shown there.
Revoke the token at the registry, since it was stored in the open.
For publishing, use a short-lived token or sign in again when needed.

sc.yarn.settings.name: Yarn protections
sc.yarn.settings.titleFail: A Yarn protection is switched off
sc.yarn.settings.why: TLS and checksum checks make sure a package is the one the registry published. Install scripts are how most malicious packages do their damage.
fix: Open .yarnrc.yml in your user folder in a text editor.
Delete the line shown in the details, so Yarn's own default applies again.

sc.yarn.credentials.name: Yarn stored tokens
sc.yarn.credentials.titlePass: No Yarn registry tokens are stored as plain text
sc.yarn.credentials.titleFail: Yarn registry tokens are stored as plain text
sc.yarn.credentials.why: A registry token in a plain file or a permanent variable can be read by every program you run. With it, an attacker publishes packages in your name.
fix: Delete the line or variable shown in the details, or run yarn npm logout.
Revoke the token at the registry, since it was stored in the open.
If a token must be configured, write it as ${NPM_TOKEN} and set that variable only when needed.

sc.pip.settings.name: pip package sources
sc.pip.settings.titlePass: pip gets packages from one index over HTTPS
sc.pip.settings.titleFail: pip is set to trust unsafe package sources
sc.pip.settings.why: With an extra index, a public package of the same name can take a private one's place. A trusted host is one whose certificate pip no longer checks.
fix: Open the pip.ini file named in the details in a text editor.
Delete the line shown there; for a variable, delete the variable.
For a private index, use index-url alone, pointing at an index that also serves the public packages you need.

sc.pypi.credentials.name: Python index passwords
sc.pypi.credentials.titlePass: No Python index passwords are stored as plain text
sc.pypi.credentials.titleFail: A Python index password is stored as plain text
sc.pypi.credentials.why: A password or token in a plain file can be read by every program you run. With a publishing token, an attacker releases packages in your name.
fix: Delete the password or token from the file named in the details.
Revoke it at the index, since it was stored in the open.
Publish with a short-lived token or trusted publishing; keep other passwords in your password manager or keyring.

sc.env.tls.name: TLS checks in variables
sc.env.tls.titlePass: No variable switches off TLS certificate checks
sc.env.tls.titleFail: A variable switches off TLS certificate checks
sc.env.tls.why: With certificate checks off, a tool accepts packages and code from anyone who can sit between you and the server.
fix: Press Start, type environment variables, and open Edit environment variables for your account.
Delete the variable named in the details.
If a company proxy needs it, ask IT for the proxy's certificate and trust that instead.

sc.env.injection.name: Code loaded by variables
sc.env.injection.titlePass: No variable loads code into your development tools
sc.env.injection.titleFail: A variable loads code into every program of one kind
sc.env.injection.why: Such a variable makes every Node.js, .NET or Java program run extra code first. Malware sets it to stay on a PC unseen.
fix: Press Start, type environment variables, and open Edit environment variables for your account.
Find the variable named in the details and check which tool set it.
Delete it unless you know the tool and still use it.

sc.env.tokens.name: Secrets in variables
sc.env.tokens.titlePass: No permanent variable holds a token or password
sc.env.tokens.titleFail: Permanent variables hold tokens or passwords
sc.env.tokens.why: Every program you run inherits these variables. A malicious package's install script reads them first.
fix: Press Start, type environment variables, and open Edit environment variables for your account.
Delete the variable named in the details.
Revoke the token where it was issued, and keep the new one in your password manager.

sc.git.settings.name: Git protections
sc.git.settings.titleFail: A Git setting switches off a protection
sc.git.settings.why: These settings decide whether a clone can be tampered with on the way, or run something you did not ask for.
fix: Open the file named in the details in a text editor.
Delete the line shown there, or the whole section if nothing else is in it.
If one server needs an exception, limit it to that server's address instead of all.

sc.git.credentials.name: Git stored passwords
sc.git.credentials.titlePass: Git keeps no passwords in plain files
sc.git.credentials.titleFail: Git keeps passwords in plain files
sc.git.credentials.why: A password or token in a plain file can be read by every program you run. With it, an attacker pushes code in your name.
fix: Run git config --global credential.helper manager so that Windows keeps the passwords.
Delete the file named in the details.
Revoke the tokens that were in it where they were issued, then sign in again.

sc.nuget.sources.name: NuGet package sources
sc.nuget.sources.titlePass: NuGet gets packages from sources it can trust
sc.nuget.sources.titleFail: A NuGet setting weakens where packages come from
sc.nuget.sources.why: With several sources and no mapping, a public package can take the place of a private one of the same name.
fix: Open the NuGet.Config file named in the details.
Change a source that starts with http:// to https://, and remove disableTLSCertificateValidation.
With more than one source, add a packageSourceMapping section that ties package names to a source.

sc.nuget.credentials.name: NuGet stored passwords
sc.nuget.credentials.titlePass: NuGet keeps no passwords as plain text
sc.nuget.credentials.titleFail: NuGet keeps a source's password as plain text
sc.nuget.credentials.why: A password in a plain file can be read by every program you run. It gives them your access to the private feed.
fix: Remove the source with dotnet nuget remove source followed by its name.
Add it again with dotnet nuget add source, without --store-password-in-clear-text.
Change the password or token, since it was stored in the open.

sc.nuget.cooldown.name: NuGet release cooldown
sc.nuget.cooldown.titlePass: NuGet waits a week before picking new versions
sc.nuget.cooldown.titleFail: NuGet picks new package versions at once
sc.nuget.cooldown.why: Most malicious package versions are found and removed within days. A week's wait keeps them out of your builds.
fix: Open the NuGet.Config file named in the details.
Add minPublishAgeHours="168" to each source's line under packageSources.
Update the .NET SDK to 11.0.100 or later if the details say it is older.

sc.github.credentials.name: GitHub CLI token
sc.github.credentials.titlePass: The GitHub CLI keeps no token in a plain file
sc.github.credentials.titleFail: The GitHub CLI keeps its token in a plain file
sc.github.credentials.why: A GitHub token in a plain file can be read by every program you run. With it, an attacker pushes code in your name.
fix: Run gh auth logout, then gh auth login, without --insecure-storage.
Check that hosts.yml no longer has an oauth_token line.
Revoke the old token under GitHub Settings, Applications.

sc.docker.settings.name: Docker protections
sc.docker.settings.titlePass: Docker checks TLS and keeps its control port closed
sc.docker.settings.titleFail: A Docker setting switches off a protection
sc.docker.settings.why: A registry without TLS checks can hand you a tampered image. An open control port gives anyone who reaches it your PC.
fix: In Docker Desktop, open Settings, General, and switch off Expose daemon on tcp://localhost:2375 without TLS.
Under Settings, Docker Engine, remove the insecure-registries and hosts lines.
Select Apply and restart.

sc.docker.credentials.name: Docker stored sign-ins
sc.docker.credentials.titlePass: Docker keeps no registry passwords in a plain file
sc.docker.credentials.titleFail: Docker keeps registry passwords in a plain file
sc.docker.credentials.why: Without a credential store, docker login writes the password into a file every program can read, only encoded.
fix: Run docker logout for each registry named in the details.
Open config.json in your .docker folder and set "credsStore": "wincred".
Run docker login again, and change the passwords that were in the file.

sc.cloud.credentials.name: Cloud keys in files
sc.cloud.credentials.titlePass: No long-lived cloud keys are stored as plain text
sc.cloud.credentials.titleFail: Long-lived cloud keys are stored as plain text
sc.cloud.credentials.why: A cloud key in a plain file can be read by every program you run. It works from anywhere until someone revokes it.
fix: Switch the tool named in the details to a sign-in that expires, such as aws sso login.
Delete the key or token from the file shown.
Revoke the old key in the cloud console.

sc.build.credentials.name: Build tool passwords
sc.build.credentials.titlePass: Build tools keep no passwords as plain text
sc.build.credentials.titleFail: Build tools keep passwords as plain text
sc.build.credentials.why: A repository password or publishing key in a plain file can be read by every program you run, build scripts included.
fix: Remove the entry shown in the details from its file.
Use the tool's own encryption or a variable set only when publishing.
Change the password or key, since it was stored in the open.

sc.editor.updates.name: Editor extension updates
sc.editor.updates.titlePass: Your editor waits before installing extension updates
sc.editor.updates.titleFail: Your editor installs extension updates within hours
sc.editor.updates.why: An extension runs with all your rights. When one is taken over, the malicious update reaches every PC that updates at once.
fix: In the editor, open Settings and search for extensions.autoUpdateDelay.
Set it to 168. In Cursor, set extensions.installCooldownHours to 168 instead.
If the setting is missing, update the editor, or switch Extensions: Auto Update off.

sc.editor.settings.name: Editor protections
sc.editor.settings.titleFail: An editor protection is switched off
sc.editor.settings.why: These settings stand between opening a downloaded folder and running its code with all your rights.
fix: In the editor, open Settings and search for the setting named in the details.
Select the gear beside it, then Reset Setting.
Do the same in each profile that the details name.

sc.mcp.servers.name: MCP servers
sc.mcp.servers.titlePass: No MCP server runs unpinned code
sc.mcp.servers.titleFail: An MCP server runs unpinned code or exposes a secret
sc.mcp.servers.why: An MCP server runs with all your rights. Without a fixed version, whoever takes over the package runs code here at the next start.
fix: Open the settings file named in the details.
Add an exact version to the package, such as name@1.2.3 for npx or name==1.2.3 for uvx.
Replace a secret written in the file with a reference to a variable, and change that secret.

sc.agents.permissions.name: AI tool approvals
sc.agents.permissions.titlePass: AI coding tools ask before they act
sc.agents.permissions.titleFail: An AI coding tool acts without asking
sc.agents.permissions.why: With asking switched off, text the tool reads in a web page or a repository can make it run commands with all your rights.
fix: Open the settings file named in the details.
Delete the line shown there.
Use the no-asking mode only per session, inside a container or a virtual machine.

sc.winget.policies.name: winget verification
sc.winget.policies.titlePass: No policy weakens what winget verifies
sc.winget.policies.titleFail: A policy lets winget skip a verification
sc.winget.policies.why: winget checks an installer's hash and scans archives before it installs. With a check switched off, a tampered download gets through.
fix: These settings come from your organisation's policy, so ask IT to review them.
Name the policy shown in the details when you ask.

sc.choco.settings.name: Chocolatey verification
sc.choco.settings.titleFail: A Chocolatey setting weakens what it verifies
sc.choco.settings.why: Chocolatey compares each download with a checksum from the package. Without that, a swapped download installs unnoticed.
fix: Open a terminal as administrator.
Run choco feature enable -n checksumFiles and choco feature disable -n allowEmptyChecksums.
Remove a source over plain HTTP with choco source remove -n followed by its name.

sc.go.settings.name: Go module verification
sc.go.settings.titlePass: Go verifies the modules it downloads
sc.go.settings.titleFail: A Go setting weakens how modules are verified
sc.go.settings.why: Go compares every module with a public checksum database. With that off, a tampered module builds into your program unnoticed.
fix: Run go env -u followed by the setting named in the details, such as GOINSECURE or GOSUMDB.
If it is a permanent variable instead, delete it under Edit environment variables for your account.
For private modules, list only your own hosts in GOPRIVATE.

sc.cargo.settings.name: Cargo crate sources
sc.cargo.settings.titlePass: Cargo gets crates from sources it can trust
sc.cargo.settings.titleFail: A Cargo setting weakens where crates come from
sc.cargo.settings.why: Over plain HTTP, or with revoked certificates accepted, a crate can be swapped on its way to your build.
fix: Open the config.toml file named in the details.
Delete the check-revoke line, and change a registry address from http:// to https://.
If a variable is named instead, delete it under Edit environment variables for your account.

sc.cargo.credentials.name: Cargo stored tokens
sc.cargo.credentials.titlePass: Cargo keeps no registry tokens as plain text
sc.cargo.credentials.titleFail: Cargo keeps registry tokens as plain text
sc.cargo.credentials.why: A registry token in a plain file can be read by every program you run. With it, an attacker publishes crates in your name.
fix: Run cargo logout to remove the token from the file.
Add global-credential-providers = ["cargo:wincred"] under [registry] in config.toml.
Revoke the old token at the registry, then run cargo login again.

sc.trust.rootcerts.name: Certificate authorities for your account
sc.trust.rootcerts.titlePass: Certificate authorities added for your account are listed
sc.trust.rootcerts.titleFail: A certificate authority was added for your account
sc.trust.rootcerts.why: Whoever holds the key of a trusted certificate authority can pose as any website or package registry to you.
fix: Press Start, type certmgr.msc and open it.
Open Trusted Root Certification Authorities, Certificates, and find the thumbprint from the details.
Delete the certificate unless you know which tool added it and still use that tool.

sc.defender.exclusions.name: Defender exclusions
sc.defender.exclusions.titleFail: Microsoft Defender skips where downloaded code lands
sc.defender.exclusions.why: Defender does not scan what is excluded. A malicious package in an excluded folder runs without ever being looked at.
fix: Open Windows Security, Virus & threat protection, Manage settings.
Under Exclusions, select Add or remove exclusions.
Remove the entries named in the details, or narrow them to single files.

sc.malware.installed.name: Known-malicious packages (installed)
sc.malware.installed.titlePass: No installed package is known to be malicious
sc.malware.installed.why: Malicious packages steal tokens and keys from the PC they run on. One that is installed has most likely already run.
fix: Look up the id from the details at osv.dev to see what the package does.
Remove the package or extension with the tool that installed it.
Change every password, token and key this PC could reach, starting with those the advisory names.
Tell your IT or security contact.

sc.malware.downloaded.name: Known-malicious packages (downloaded)
sc.malware.downloaded.titlePass: No downloaded package is known to be malicious
sc.malware.downloaded.why: A package in a download cache was fetched at some point and may have run. Malicious packages steal tokens and keys from the PC they run on.
fix: Look up the id from the details at osv.dev to see what the package does.
Find the project that asked for it and remove or pin the dependency.
Clear the cache named in the details with its own tool, for example uv cache clean.
If it may have run, change the passwords, tokens and keys this PC could reach and tell IT.

sc.malware.list.name: List of known-malicious packages
sc.malware.list.titlePass: The list of known-malicious packages is recent
sc.malware.list.titleFail: The list of known-malicious packages is out of date
sc.malware.list.why: New malicious packages are reported every day. An old list misses the ones most likely to reach you now.
fix: Install the latest version of SecReview, which carries a current list.
